To overegg the pudding means to overdo something — to add more than is needed, usually to make something seem better, more impressive, or more dramatic than it really is. The result of this "overdoing" is that things actually get worse, not better. The exaggeration becomes obvious, and people stop believing you or taking you seriously.

Think of it this way: it means trying too hard to improve something, and in doing so, ruining it.

The idiom comes straight from the kitchen — specifically, from British cooking.

In British cuisine, a "pudding" isn't just what Americans call pudding (a creamy dessert). It's a broader term for many kinds of baked or steamed dishes, both sweet (like a sponge pudding) and savoury. Eggs are a critical ingredient in these recipes. They bind the ingredients together and give the pudding its texture — light, airy, and just right.

Now, here's the key: eggs only work well in the right amount. If you add the correct number of eggs, your pudding comes out perfectly. But if you think, "More eggs = better pudding," and you start cracking in extra eggs, something goes wrong. The pudding becomes rubbery, heavy, and unpleasant. Your good intention has backfired completely. You tried to make it better, but you made it worse.

That is the heart of this idiom. Just as adding too many eggs ruins a pudding, overdoing anything — especially exaggerating or over-embellishing — ruins the thing you're trying to improve.
The Key Idea: It Always Backfires

This is the most important nuance to understand: overegging the pudding doesn't just mean adding extra — it means the extra addition causes harm. The excess defeats the purpose.

This is what separates this idiom from simply saying "too much." It specifically implies:

  1. You were trying to enhance or improve something.
  2. You went beyond what was needed.
  3. Because of that excess, the result is now less convincing, less effective, or less believable.

The idiom is flexible. You can overegg the pudding in many different situations:

  • Exaggerating a story — You add so many dramatic details that people roll their eyes and don't believe the core truth anymore.
  • Over-praising something — You describe a product, person, or event in such glowing terms that it sounds fake and untrustworthy.
  • Over-decorating or over-designing — You add so many features, colours, or elements that the end result looks cluttered and messy.
  • Making an argument too forcefully — You pile on so many points, so many statistics, and so much emotion that your argument feels desperate rather than convincing.
  • Over-acting — A performer exaggerates their expressions and gestures so much that the audience laughs instead of feeling moved.

In every case, the person's effort to strengthen something has weakened it instead.

Here are examples to see how the idiom works in sentences:

  • "His speech was good, but he overegged the pudding by repeating the same point five times. People started getting bored."
    → He made the speech longer and more forceful than it needed to be, and it hurt rather than helped.
  • "The advertisement overegged the pudding — calling a basic smartphone 'the most revolutionary device in human history' just made people laugh."
    → The exaggerated praise destroyed the ad's credibility.
  • "She overegged the pudding on her CV by listing skills she barely had. When the interviewer asked about them, she was embarrassed."
    → Embellishing her qualifications beyond reality backfired badly.
  • "The cake was already delicious. Adding three layers of extra frosting was overegging the pudding — now it's sickly sweet."
    → A literal near-example. Something already good was made worse by unnecessary additions.
  • "The film's ending was emotional, but the director overegged the pudding with that ten-minute crying scene. It went from moving to melodramatic."
    → Too much emotional intensity undermined the very emotion the director was aiming for.
A Subtle but Important Point: Intention vs. Result

Notice that when someone overeggs the pudding, their intention is usually good. They want to:

  • Make their story more interesting.
  • Make their product sound more appealing.
  • Make their argument more persuasive.

They are not lying for the sake of lying. They genuinely believe that "more" will help. But because they misjudge how much is "too much," the result is the opposite of what they hoped for. This is why the idiom often carries a slightly sympathetic but also critical tone — it's a gentle or pointed way of saying, "You tried too hard, and it didn't work."
Tone and Register: When Do People Use It?

This idiom is informal, but not slang. It sits comfortably in:

  • Everyday conversation
  • Journalism and opinion writing
  • Politics (it's particularly popular among British politicians and commentators)
  • Reviews of films, books, restaurants, or performances

It is predominantly British English. If you say it to an American, they may not immediately understand it. An equivalent American expression would be something like "laying it on too thick" or "gilding the lily" (though these have slightly different flavours, explained below).
How Is It Different From Similar Expressions?

"Laying it on thick" — This means flattering someone excessively or being overly complimentary, often to manipulate them. It's more focused on praise and flattery specifically. "Overegging the pudding" is broader — it applies to any kind of excess, not just flattery.

"Gilding the lily" — This means adding unnecessary decoration or improvement to something that is already perfect. The difference is subtle but real: gilding the lily is about doing something pointless (the lily is already beautiful; gold paint is unnecessary but doesn't necessarily make it ugly). Overegging the pudding is about doing something that actively makes things worse. One is wasteful; the other is counterproductive.

"Going overboard" — This means doing too much of something in a general sense. It's less specific about the idea that the excess harms credibility or quality. "Overegging the pudding" has that specific sense of undermining the thing you're trying to strengthen.
A Quick Formula to Remember It

If you want a mental shortcut, remember this:

Overegging the pudding = Well-intentioned excess + Backfiring result

You tried to make something better. You added too much. Now it's worse — and probably less believable.

"Overegg the pudding" means to exaggerate or overdo something so much — in an attempt to make it better — that you actually make it worse, often by making it seem unbelievable, excessive, or ridiculous.
